title: A Saucerful of Secrets
label: EMI Columbia · Tower
overview:
Recorded in 1967 and 1968 at EMI Studios and De Lane Lea Studios in London with the producer Norman Smith, and released on 28 June 1968 by EMI Columbia in the UK and by Tower Records, a division of Capitol, in the US. David Gilmour joined in December 1967 as a fifth member and Syd Barrett left in late January 1968, so the album is a transition: Barrett is credited on three tracks ("Remember a Day", "Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun" and "Jugband Blues", the last of them his only composition here) and Gilmour plays guitar on the rest. Richard Wright plays Farfisa organ on every track, with Hammond organ, Mellotron, piano, vibraphone, celesta and xylophone on individual tracks. The album reached UK No. 9 and is certified Gold in the UK by the BPI; in the US it did not chart until 2019, when a mono reissue reached No. 158. The cover is by Storm Thorgerson of Hipgnosis, the first of several Pink Floyd covers by that group.

Side one holds four songs, and side two opens with the 11:57 four-movement instrumental title track, followed by "See-Saw" and "Jugband Blues".

Section timestamps are measured on a rip of the CD and are approximate to ±5 seconds.

tracks.title: Let There Be More Light
tracks.role: Album role: The album opener, built on a bass riff that came from "Interstellar Overdrive", and the A-side of the US single released on 19 August 1968 with "Remember a Day" on the reverse.

events.description: The track opens at a moderate level and the top end fills in within the first few seconds.
events.detail: Wikipedia says the song evolved from a bass riff that was part of "Interstellar Overdrive", and that a jam recorded on 18 January 1968 formed its intro; it credits Richard Wright with Hammond organ and piano on this track.

events.description: The level falls and the top end thins out for about half a minute, the first big change in the track.
Loud and quiet passages alternate in short blocks of roughly 10 to 25 seconds, four loud blocks against four quiet ones.
The alternation stops and a steady, fuller texture runs for about a minute and a half.
The level and the low end fall away and the track fades out.

tracks.title: Remember a Day
tracks.role: Album role: A Wright song placed second, an outtake from The Piper at the Gates of Dawn that received Barrett's slide guitar overdub, and the reverse side of the US single.

events.description: A quiet, gradual fade-in, reaching full level after about 20 seconds.
events.detail: Wikipedia says Syd Barrett overdubbed slide guitar onto this outtake from The Piper at the Gates of Dawn and that Norman Smith plays drums on it, with Nick Mason absent from the track.

events.description: The level falls for about ten seconds, then the top end opens at 1:02.
A shorter dip in level before a long steady stretch begins at 1:57.
A long, even passage with a regular pulse runs for over a minute.
The pulse nearly disappears for about 15 seconds while the bass swells, then returns.
The pulse and the low end return, and the track reaches its loudest level before 4:00.
The level falls and the track fades out.

tracks.title: Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun
tracks.role: Album role: The slow, hypnotic centrepiece of side one, first performed live with Barrett in 1967 and finished with Waters's vocal and Wright's organ in January 1968.

events.description: The track fades in from near silence and the level climbs steadily for the first 40 seconds.
events.detail: Wikipedia credits Wright with vibraphone and celesta, Waters with percussion and Gilmour with guitar on this track, and says Waters borrowed the lyrics from Tang dynasty Chinese poetry; it dates the basic recording to 7 and 8 August 1967 and Waters's vocal and Wright's organ overdubs to sessions from 10 January 1968 at EMI.

events.description: The top end opens and the texture grows fuller until about 1:50.
The track reaches a steady, strong low end that holds for over a minute and a half.
The level and low end ease back for half a minute, then return.
A fuller stretch with a strong low end runs to the close.
The track fades out.

tracks.title: Corporal Clegg
tracks.role: Album role: The closing track of side one, a Waters song on which Nick Mason shares lead vocals and Gilmour plays kazoo.

events.description: The track fades in over the first two seconds and settles quickly.
events.detail: Wikipedia lists Mason, Gilmour and Wright on lead vocals, credits Gilmour with kazoo and Wright with Hammond organ, and lists the Stanley Myers Orchestra on this track.

events.description: The bass and the pulse step up for about ten seconds.
The top end opens sharply and the pulse grows firmer for about 25 seconds.
The top end falls away and the level eases through the middle of the track.
The top end opens again and the track reaches its loudest and brightest level, held until the end.
The sound stops, leaving a few seconds of silence.

tracks.title: A Saucerful of Secrets
tracks.role: Album role: The side two opener and the album's long instrumental centrepiece, in four movements (Something Else, Syncopated Pandemonium, Storm Signal, Celestial Voices), credited to all four of Waters, Wright, Mason and Gilmour.

events.description: The first movement, "Something Else", opens from near silence with a sparse, slow texture.
events.detail: Wikipedia gives the movement lengths as 3:57, 3:07, 1:34 and 3:19, and says the piece began as a new version of "Nick's Boogie"; it credits Wright with Mellotron, Hammond organ, vibraphone and piano, Mason and Waters with percussion, and Gilmour and Wright with wordless vocals.

events.description: The top end opens gradually and the texture fills out over the next minute.
The deepest bass drops out and the middle range takes over.
The low end comes back and the level rises toward the close of the movement.
The level drops to near silence, and about ten seconds later "Syncopated Pandemonium" begins at a much higher level with a more regular rhythmic pulse than the first movement.
The loudest passage of the second movement, followed by a drop in level at about 6:30.
"Storm Signal" begins: the low end rises and the treble falls away, giving a darker and heavier texture.
The level dips and the deepest bass is absent for several seconds.
"Celestial Voices" begins with a strong surge of deep bass and a steady, low-pitched, nearly beatless texture.
The level rises to the loudest sustained stretch of the track, which runs to the end.
The sound fades to silence.

tracks.title: See-Saw
tracks.role: Album role: A Wright song on side two, between the long title track and the closing "Jugband Blues", with a keyboard-led arrangement.

events.description: The track fades in and reaches a steady level within 20 seconds.
events.detail: Wikipedia credits Wright with piano, Mellotron and xylophone and Norman Smith with backing vocals on this track.

events.description: The level and the treble fall for about ten seconds.
The top end opens sharply and the texture brightens for a short stretch.
The pulse nearly vanishes for a few seconds, returning by 2:33.
The top end opens again and the level stays high through the rest of the track.
The level drops and the track fades out.

tracks.title: Jugband Blues
tracks.role: Album role: The album's closing track and its only song written by Syd Barrett, recorded on 19 October 1967 with a Salvation Army brass band.

events.description: The track opens at a moderate level and settles within ten seconds.
events.detail: Wikipedia says Norman Smith booked the Salvation Army International Staff Band on Barrett's recommendation, that Barrett told him to let the band play whatever they wanted, and that Smith insisted on composed parts; it credits Wright with tin whistle and Mason with kazoo.

events.description: The level rises to the loudest, brightest stretch of the track.
The low end drops out and the treble falls, leaving a thinner texture, and the bass returns strongly at 1:51.
The level falls sharply and the track continues at a much lower level, picking up a little by 2:37.
